items.text: A contractor in Wayne County sues a homeowner for $12,000 in unpaid remodeling work. Which court has exclusive jurisdiction?
A. District court — MCL 600.8301(1) gives district court exclusive jurisdiction over civil actions where the amount in controversy does not exceed $25,000.
A homeowner sues the Michigan Department of Insurance and Financial Services itself for money damages over how it handled her complaint. Which court has exclusive jurisdiction over that claim?

D. Court of Claims — MCL 600.6419(1)(a) gives the Court of Claims exclusive jurisdiction over demands for monetary, equitable, or declaratory relief against the state or any of its departments or officers, and MCL 600.6419(7) defines that phrase to include any state department or agency, which covers DIFS.
After losing a final judgment in circuit court, an insurer wants to appeal. What is true about that appeal?
C. It goes to the Court of Appeals as a matter of right — MCL 600.308(1) gives the Court of Appeals jurisdiction as of right over final judgments and final orders from the circuit court.
An adjuster cites an unpublished 2021 Court of Appeals opinion to argue a coverage point. What must the adjuster's attorney do under MCR 7.215(C)(1)?

B. Explain the reason for citing it and how it is relevant to the issues presented — MCR 7.215(C)(1) requires a party citing an unpublished opinion to explain the reason for citing it and how it is relevant.
A published Court of Appeals opinion is later the subject of an application for leave to appeal filed in the Michigan Supreme Court. What happens to its precedential effect in the meantime?

A. It is unaffected; filing the application does not diminish its precedential effect — MCR 7.215(C)(2) states that filing an application for leave to appeal, or the Supreme Court granting leave, does not diminish the precedential effect of a published opinion.
DIFS Bulletin 2024-26-INS changed how insurers handle labor depreciation. What kind of legal instrument is a DIFS bulletin?

C. Interpretive guidance that can be reissued or withdrawn by the agency without a legislative vote — A DIFS bulletin is interpretive guidance, not independent law; it can change whenever the agency reissues or withdraws it, unlike a statute which requires legislative action.
An adjuster tells a homeowner that Michigan's matching rule is found in Mich Admin Code R 500.2202. Is this correct?

D. No, R 500.2202 is titled "Discretionary Clauses Prohibited" and Michigan has no matching statute or rule — R 500.2202 is the discretionary-clauses rule, unrelated to matching; Michigan has no matching statute or administrative rule at all.
As of this run, what is the legal status of Senate Bill 245, the first-party bad-faith bill?

B. It is still pending; reported favorably from committee and referred to the Committee of the Whole, but not enacted — SB 245 was reported favorably without amendment from the Finance, Insurance, and Consumer Protection Committee on 6/17/2026 and referred to the Committee of the Whole, but has not passed either chamber or been signed.
How should the citation MCL 500.2833(1)(q) be read aloud?
A. Act 218 of 1956, section 2833, subsection 1, subdivision q — Chapter 500 is the Insurance Code of 1956, Act 218 of 1956; 2833 is the section; (1) is the subsection; (q) is the subdivision.
What does the abbreviation "Mich App" in a case citation tell you, compared to just "Mich"?
D. "Mich App" means Court of Appeals; "Mich" alone means Supreme Court — "Mich App" is the Michigan Appeals Reports (Court of Appeals); "Mich" without "App" is the Michigan Reports (Supreme Court).
A homeowner in Kent County calls DIFS demanding it force her insurer to pay a denied claim immediately. What is the accurate answer about what DIFS can do?

C. DIFS will investigate the complaint and try to help resolve it, but its Chapter 12 remedies run against licensees; it does not enter a money judgment ordering the insurer to pay her — DIFS's own complaint page describes investigating complaints and assisting consumers in resolving them whenever possible, and it encourages trying the company directly first; the Chapter 12 remedies in MCL 500.1242 and 500.1244 are license discipline, fines, refunds, and restitution against a licensee after a hearing, not a payment order against an insurer in a coverage dispute.
DIFS finds, after a hearing, that a licensed adjuster violated Chapter 12 by misrepresenting claim information. Under MCL 500.1244(1), what can the director order?

B. A cease-and-desist order plus any of: a civil fine, refund of overcharges, restitution to the insured, and suspension or revocation of the license — MCL 500.1244(1)(a)-(d) lists these remedies available to the director after a hearing finds a Chapter 12 violation.
Under MCL 500.1242, can the insurance commissioner suspend an adjuster's license without any hearing at all?

C. Yes, but only through summary suspension when the commissioner finds protection of the public requires emergency action; if the licensee requests a hearing it must be held within a reasonable time and not later than 20 days after the suspension takes effect — MCL 500.1242(4) allows summary suspension without a prior hearing when protection of the public requires emergency action; if requested, a hearing must be held within a reasonable time but not later than 20 days after the effective date unless the licensee asks for a later date, and the decision announced within 30 days after the hearing.

A pipe bursts in a Livonia home on March 1. The homeowner notifies the insurer the same day. The insurer formally denies the claim on July 1. When does the 1-year suit clock under MCL 500.2833(1)(q) actually begin running?

B. It never ran during the notice-to-denial period; her effective window runs from July 1, the date of formal denial — The statute tolls the clock from the time the insured notifies the insurer of the loss until the insurer formally denies liability; it does not run during that window.
A fire insurance policy states a suit must be filed within 8 months of loss. Under MCL 500.2833(1)(q), is that provision enforceable?

A. No, the statute sets 1 year as a floor ("whichever is longer"); a shorter contractual period does not control — MCL 500.2833(1)(q) requires 1 year after loss or the time period specified in the policy, whichever is longer, meaning a policy cannot validly shorten the period below 1 year.

A non-lawyer advertises himself as a "claims attorney" and offers to represent homeowners in coverage disputes without a Michigan law license. Which statute does this violate, and what is the consequence?

D. MCL 600.916(1); contempt of the supreme court and of the circuit court where the violation occurred — MCL 600.916(1) prohibits holding oneself out as an attorney without a license, and the consequence is contempt of the supreme court and of the circuit court of the county where the violation occurred.
A restoration contractor argues that because his brother-in-law is a licensed Michigan attorney, he personally is exempt from adjuster licensing under MCL 500.1222(2)(a). Is he correct?

B. No, the exemption in MCL 500.1222(2)(a) reaches only a person who is themselves admitted to the practice of law in Michigan — MCL 500.1222(2)(a) exempts "a person admitted to the practice of law in this state," meaning the exemption applies only to the licensed attorney personally, not to associates or relatives.
An out-of-state attorney, licensed only in Ohio, comes to Michigan briefly to handle one specific matter for a client. Under MCL 600.916, is this unauthorized practice of law?

A. No, the statute exempts an attorney licensed in another state while temporarily in Michigan and engaged in a particular matter — MCL 600.916(1) explicitly exempts a person duly licensed to practice law in another state while temporarily in Michigan and engaged in a particular matter.
In a coverage dispute where the facts about what happened are not really contested and the only question is whether an exclusion applies as a matter of law, which motion is most likely?

C. A motion for summary disposition under MCR 2.116(C)(10) — MCR 2.116(C)(10) allows the court to grant judgment without trial when there is no genuine issue of material fact and the moving party is entitled to judgment as a matter of law.
A public adjuster wants to sue an insurer directly in Michigan's Court of Claims over a private homeowner's denied claim. Is the Court of Claims the correct venue?

D. No, the Court of Claims has exclusive jurisdiction only over claims against the State of Michigan or its departments and officers, not a private insurer — MCL 600.6419(1) limits Court of Claims jurisdiction to claims against the state and its departments or officers; a private insurer is not the state, so the suit belongs in circuit court.
